ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
In a circular region with radius \( R \), there exists a uniform magnetic field with magnetic induction \( B \), directed perpendicularly into the plane of the paper. A negatively charged particle (ignoring gravity) enters horizontally with velocity \( v \) directly toward the center. After passing through the magnetic field region, the direction of its velocity is deflected by \( 60^{\circ} \).

1. What is the specific charge $\frac{q}{m}$ of the particle?
2. What is the time $t$ for the motion of a particle in a magnetic field?
3. If the magnitude and direction of the velocity remain unchanged, how much should the incident point of the particle be shifted upward along the arc by a distance $d$ in order to maximize the deflection angle of the velocity direction after the particle passes through the magnetic field region?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure there is a circular region, and inside the circle there are many “×” symbols, indicating that the magnetic field is perpendicular to the paper surface inward; the center of the circle is labeled O, and the radius is labeled R. On the left side there is a velocity v with an arrow incident horizontally to the right, and the incident direction is along the horizontal dashed line passing through the center O, indicating that the particle enters from the left end of the circle and points directly toward the center. Reasoning: According to the problem statement, take the center O as the coordinate origin, and when it has not initially moved upward, the incident point is A=(-R,0). A negative charge enters to the right with velocity, and the magnetic field is inward. From the direction of the Lorentz force, it can be known that the center C of the circular-motion trajectory of the particle in the magnetic field is directly below A. Let the trajectory radius CA=ρ. At this time OC=sqrt(R^2+ρ^2). When the particle leaves the magnetic field, the deflection angle of the velocity direction is equal to the central angle θ corresponding to the trajectory center C; since the intersection points of the two circles are symmetric about OC, ∠ACO=θ/2. Therefore cos(θ/2)=ρ/OC=ρ/sqrt(R^2+ρ^2). It is known that θ=60°, so cos30°=ρ/sqrt(R^2+ρ^2). That is, sqrt(3)/2=ρ/sqrt(R^2+ρ^2), solving gives ρ=sqrt(3)R. The circular-motion radius in the magnetic field satisfies ρ=mv/(|q|B), so |q|/m=v/(Bρ)=v/(B sqrt(3)R)=sqrt(3)v/(3BR). If q is strictly taken as the signed charge quantity, then q/m=-sqrt(3)v/(3BR); usually the “specific charge” takes the magnitude, consistent with the standard answer as sqrt(3)v/(3BR). The magnitude of the angular velocity of the particle in the magnetic field is ω=v/ρ. The central angle turned through when passing through the magnetic field is θ=π/3, so the motion time t=θ/ω=(π/3)ρ/v=(π/3)(sqrt(3)R)/v=sqrt(3)πR/(3v). If the incident point moves upward along the circumference, according to the method let the new incident point be A=(-sqrt(R^2-d^2), d), and the trajectory center C is still a distance ρ below A. Thus OC^2=R^2+ρ^2-2ρd. Similarly from the geometric relationship of the intersection of two circles, if the deflection angle is θ, then cos(θ/2)=(ρ-d)/OC=(ρ-d)/sqrt(R^2+ρ^2-2ρd). To make the deflection angle θ maximum, it is necessary to make cos(θ/2) minimum. Let f(d)=(ρ-d)/sqrt(R^2+ρ^2-2ρd). Differentiation gives that the sign of f'(d) is determined by ρd-R^2, and the extremum condition is ρd-R^2=0, so d=R^2/ρ. Substituting ρ=sqrt(3)R gives d=R^2/(sqrt(3)R)=R/sqrt(3)=sqrt(3)R/3.
